questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: In a study of whether study time affects exam scores, which variable is the dependent variable?

options.misconception: confuses the manipulated factor with the measured outcome
confuses a design feature with the measured variable
confuses a controlled condition with the measured variable

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome being measured, which is exam scores. Study time is the independent variable because it is manipulated, and the number of participants and the type of exam are design features, so each distractor names a real feature of the study applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: Which variable is measured as the outcome?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A researcher compares two diets and measures weight loss, but does not record participants' exercise habits. What is the most likely threat to the conclusion?

options.text: Exercise habits act as an uncontrolled confound
The sample size is too small
options.misconception: attributes the problem to sample size without evidence
assumes diet similarity is the issue
claims the outcome is unmeasurable

questions.explanation: Exercise habits vary alongside diet and also affect weight loss, so they confound the diet effect. The other options introduce concerns not stated in the scenario: sample size, diet similarity, and measurability are all unsupported by the description.
questions.hint: What else influences weight loss and differs across groups?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which statement best describes an operational definition?

options.text: It specifies exactly how a variable is measured or manipulated
It states the general theory behind a variable
options.misconception: confuses theory with measurement procedure

options.text: It lists the hypotheses of the study
options.misconception: confuses hypotheses with measurement rules

options.text: It names the population under study
options.misconception: confuses population with measurement rules

questions.explanation: An operational definition translates an abstract concept into concrete measurement or manipulation steps. Theory, hypotheses, and population each describe other parts of a study rather than how a variable is observed or controlled.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study randomly assigns participants to a treatment group or a control group and measures outcomes afterward. Which design is this?

options.misconception: ignores the random assignment feature
confuses association with manipulation
confuses a single time point with randomization

questions.explanation: Random assignment to treatment and control groups defines a randomized controlled trial. Quasi-experimental designs lack random assignment, correlational designs do not manipulate variables, and cross-sectional surveys capture a single time point without randomization.
questions.hint: Look for random assignment to conditions.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which design can best support a causal claim that X causes Y?

options.text: A correlational study measuring X and Y
options.misconception: confuses association with causation

options.text: A descriptive case study of one person
options.misconception: generalizes from a single case

options.text: A cross-sectional survey at one time
options.misconception: confuses snapshot data with manipulation

questions.explanation: Causal claims require manipulation and random assignment, which a randomized experiment provides. Correlational, case study, and cross-sectional designs observe without manipulation, so they cannot establish causation.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A school introduces a new reading program in one grade and compares outcomes with the previous year's grade. What design is this?

options.misconception: overlooks the lack of random assignment
assumes randomization exists
confuses repeated measures with comparison

questions.explanation: There is an intervention and a comparison, but no random assignment of participants, so this is quasi-experimental. A true experiment and randomized controlled trial both require random assignment, and a longitudinal cohort study follows the same group over time rather than comparing cohorts.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which sampling method gives every member of the population a known, nonzero chance of selection?

options.misconception: confuses ease of access with random chance
confuses judgment-based selection with probability
confuses referral chains with random selection

questions.explanation: Simple random sampling is a probability method in which each population member has a known chance of selection. Convenience, purposive, and snowball sampling are non-probability methods that do not guarantee known selection probabilities.
questions.hint: Probability sampling needs known selection chances.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A researcher divides a population into subgroups by age and then randomly selects participants from each subgroup. What is this called?

options.misconception: confuses groups sampled whole with groups sampled within
confuses ordered selection with subgroup division
confuses non-probability quotas with random strata

questions.explanation: Dividing the population into strata and sampling randomly within each stratum is stratified random sampling. Cluster sampling selects whole clusters, systematic sampling selects at fixed intervals, and quota sampling fills quotas without random selection.
questions.hint: Subgroups are strata; sampling occurs within each.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A survey recruits participants only from a university campus to estimate national opinions. What is the main concern?

options.text: The sample is not representative of the population

options.misconception: attributes bias to question difficulty

options.text: The sample size is too large
options.misconception: misidentifies size as the problem
confuses length with representativeness

questions.explanation: A campus-only sample differs systematically from the national population, threatening representativeness. Question difficulty, sample size, and survey length are not the core issue raised by the recruitment method.
questions.hint: Who is missing from this sample?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: In a test comparing a new drug to a placebo, what does the null hypothesis state?

options.text: There is no difference between drug and placebo
The drug is more effective than the placebo
options.misconception: states the alternative hypothesis instead
introduces an unrelated claim
predicts an outcome rather than no effect

questions.explanation: The null hypothesis posits no effect or no difference between groups. The drug being more effective is the alternative hypothesis, while side effects and placebo improvement are not the null.
questions.hint: The null is the no-effect statement.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A p-value of 0.03 means which of the following?

options.text: If the null were true, data this extreme would be unlikely
There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
options.misconception: confuses p-value with probability of the null
confuses p-value with effect size

options.text: The result is guaranteed to replicate
options.misconception: confuses significance with replicability

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of observing data at least this extreme assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability the null is true, not an effect size, and not a guarantee of replication.
questions.hint: Condition on the null being true.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is known as which error?

options.misconception: confuses false negative with false positive
mislabels power as an error type
confuses random sampling variation with decision error

questions.explanation: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a false positive, or Type I error. Type II error is failing to reject a false null. Power is the probability of detecting a true effect, and sampling error is random variation in estimates.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is known as which error?

options.misconception: confuses false positive with false negative
mislabels the significance level as an error
confuses the probability of Type II error with the error itself

questions.explanation: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is a false negative, or Type II error. Type I error is rejecting a true null. Alpha is the threshold for Type I error, and beta is the probability of a Type II error rather than the error itself.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which factor most directly increases statistical power?

options.misconception: confuses lax threshold with legitimate power gain
confuses noise with power

options.text: Using a one-tailed test without justification
options.misconception: confuses directional testing with power

questions.explanation: Larger samples reduce sampling variability and increase power. Raising alpha to 0.50 is not standard practice, decreasing precision lowers power, and one-tailed tests only increase power when the direction is truly predetermined.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Internal validity refers to which of the following?

options.text: Whether the study establishes a causal relationship
Whether results generalize to other populations
options.misconception: confuses internal with external validity

options.text: Whether measures reflect the intended construct
options.misconception: confuses internal with construct validity
confuses validity with significance

questions.explanation: Internal validity concerns whether the observed effect is truly caused by the independent variable rather than confounds. Generalizability is external validity, construct reflection is construct validity, and significance is a statistical matter.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Construct validity asks whether a measure actually captures which of the following?

options.text: The theoretical concept it is intended to measure

options.misconception: confuses construct with internal validity
confuses construct with external validity
confuses validity with significance testing

questions.explanation: Construct validity concerns whether the operational measure represents the intended theoretical concept. Causation is internal validity, generalizability is external validity, and significance is statistical.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: External validity is most concerned with which question?

options.text: Can these findings be generalized beyond this study?
Did the manipulation cause the effect?
options.misconception: confuses external with internal validity

options.text: Does the measure reflect the construct?
options.misconception: confuses external with construct validity
confuses validity with statistical accuracy

questions.explanation: External validity concerns generalization to other populations, settings, and times. Causation is internal validity, construct reflection is construct validity, and computation correctness is a separate issue.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: In a study, the effect of a training program on performance is stronger for novices than for experts. What role does expertise level play?

options.misconception: confuses a moderator with a mediator
misidentifies expertise as the outcome
confuses an effect modifier with a confound

questions.explanation: A variable that changes the strength or direction of a relationship is a moderator. A mediator explains the mechanism, the dependent variable is the outcome, and a confound is an extraneous influence not of interest.
questions.hint: Does it change the strength of the effect?

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A training program improves performance because it increases self-efficacy, which then improves performance. What role does self-efficacy play?

options.misconception: confuses a mediator with a moderator
misidentifies the mechanism as manipulated
confuses a mechanism with a controlled factor

questions.explanation: Self-efficacy transmits the effect of training on performance, making it a mediator. A moderator would change the strength of the effect, an independent variable is manipulated, and a control variable is held constant.
questions.hint: Does it explain how the effect occurs?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A researcher follows the same group of children from age 5 to age 15, measuring reading ability each year. What design is this?

options.misconception: confuses multiple time points with one time point
confuses follow-up with retrospective comparison
confuses observation with manipulation

questions.explanation: Following the same participants over multiple time points is longitudinal. Cross-sectional collects data at one time, case-control compares groups retrospectively, and randomized experiment requires manipulation.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study measures reading ability in children of different ages at a single point in time. What design is this?

options.misconception: confuses one time point with follow-up
confuses age groups with followed cohorts
confuses observation with manipulation

questions.explanation: Collecting data from different ages at one time point is cross-sectional. Longitudinal and cohort designs follow participants over time, and experimental designs involve manipulation.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A researcher randomly selects 10 schools and surveys all students within them. What sampling method is this?

options.misconception: confuses whole clusters with strata sampled within
confuses school-level selection with individual selection
confuses random clusters with fixed intervals

questions.explanation: Randomly selecting entire groups (clusters) and including all members is cluster sampling. Stratified sampling samples within strata, simple random sampling selects individuals directly, and systematic sampling uses fixed intervals.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: When is a one-tailed hypothesis test most appropriate?

options.text: When the research question specifies a direction of effect
When the sample size is small
options.misconception: confuses sample size with directionality
confuses significance threshold with directionality
confuses surprise with a directional prediction

questions.explanation: A one-tailed test is justified only when a specific direction is predicted before data collection. Small sample size, alpha level, and unexpected results do not justify one-tailed testing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Participants improve on a test simply because they took a similar pretest. Which threat to internal validity is this?

options.misconception: confuses natural change with practice from testing
confuses external events with pretest practice
confuses extreme-score regression with practice effects

questions.explanation: Improvement due to prior exposure to a similar test is a testing effect. Maturation is natural change over time, history is external events, and regression to the mean is score movement toward the average.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A highly controlled lab experiment produces results that may not apply to everyday settings. Which validity is most at risk?

options.misconception: confuses generalizability with causation
confuses setting generalization with measurement
confuses generalization with statistical power

questions.explanation: When lab control limits real-world applicability, external validity is threatened. Internal validity concerns causation, construct validity concerns measurement of concepts, and statistical conclusion validity concerns statistical inference.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A study plans 4 groups with 15 participants each. How many total participants are needed?
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of groups by participants per group: 4 times 15 equals 60 total participants.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A population has 500 members and a sample of 50 is selected. What is the sampling fraction as a decimal?
questions.explanation: Divide sample size by population size: 50 divided by 500 equals 0.1.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: In an experiment on fertilizer and plant growth, which variable should be held constant across groups?

options.misconception: confuses the independent variable with a control
confuses the dependent variable with a control
confuses an outcome with a controlled factor

questions.explanation: Sunlight should be held constant so it does not confound the fertilizer effect. Fertilizer type is the independent variable, and plant height and growth rate are outcomes.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A new screening test is validated by comparing its scores with an established gold-standard test. Which validity is being assessed?

options.misconception: confuses item coverage with comparison to a standard
confuses appearance with empirical comparison
confuses theoretical concept with empirical criterion

questions.explanation: Comparing a measure to an established standard assesses criterion validity. Content validity concerns item coverage, face validity concerns apparent suitability, and construct validity concerns theoretical concepts.

provenance.author: bank-team-rm3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A math test is reviewed by experts to ensure it covers all required topics and skills. Which validity is being assessed?

options.misconception: confuses topic coverage with comparison to a standard
confuses expert review of coverage with apparent suitability
confuses topic coverage with theoretical concept

questions.explanation: Expert review ensuring a measure covers the full domain of content assesses content validity. Criterion validity compares to a standard, face validity concerns appearance, and construct validity concerns theoretical concepts.
questions.hint: Does it cover the whole domain?
